chunks: Biggest efficiency loss sources in a buck. The question: What components are most responsible for efficiency losses?
The biggest losses in a buck at normal load are usually the two switches (FETs) and the inductor. The capacitors and the feedback network waste very little.
The ranking can change with the load, input voltage and frequency, so you always ask "at what operating point?"
Think of two runners passing one heavy baton back and forth. Holding it wears out their hands a little. The runner who holds it longest gets the most wear.
In a buck the low-side FET is on most of the time when the output is much lower than the input, so it handles the most current-time. The analogy fits conduction loss only.
Switching loss hits the high-side FET hardest, because it changes state against the full input voltage.
On log-log axes, the I squared terms are steep lines; the fixed terms are flat. Below about 0.

5 amps the flat and linear groups (switching/recovery, inductor core, gate and I q ) dominate and total 100 to 150 milliwatts regardless of load; above about 1 amps the FET conduction takes over and at 5 amps it is 58% of the loss.
Efficiency is the ratio of output power to output plus these curves, hence the familiar hill-shaped efficiency curve.
Conduction loss: heat from current through a resistance, I to the 2R . Switching loss: energy lost during each on/off transition.
High-side / low-side FET: the top switch (connects to V in ) and the bottom switch (connects to ground) ("Buck power bridge type and why").
DCR: the DC resistance of the inductor winding. Fixed losses: power spent just running the converter (driving the switches, powering the controller), whatever the load.
Use a 12 volts to 3. 3 volts buck at 2 amps. The top switch is on for about 3. 3 over 12 equals 27. 5 % of each cycle. Give each FET 50 milliohms.
The current is 2 amps, so I to the 2R equals 4 times 0. 05 equals 0. 2 watts while a FET is on. The high-side FET is on 27. 5% of the time, so it loses about 0. 055 watts.
The low-side FET is on 72. 5%, so about 0. 145 watts. That is the whole idea for conduction.
"At nominal load: the low-side FET (conducts 1-D of the cycle, so the biggest I to the 2R ), then the high-side FET (conduction plus all the hard switching loss), then the inductor (DCR plus core).
Capacitors and feedback are negligible. In a 12 volts to 3. 3 volts, 2 amps example, about 180, 140 and 120 milliwatts of 457 milliwatts.
The ranking shifts: at light load fixed losses (gate drive, recovery, quiescent) dominate; at high V in or high frequency switching loss dominates; at high current conduction dominates."
